title: Salt Substitutes: What They Contain and When They Are Not Equivalent to Salt

seo.title: Salt Substitutes: Potassium, Sodium, and Safety
seo.meta_description: Many salt substitutes replace some or all sodium chloride with potassium chloride. That can lower sodium, but the flavor and cooking behavior differ, and people who cannot excrete potassium normally need medical guidance.
seo.search_intent: Explain what salt substitutes contain, how potassium chloride differs from salt, and who needs caution.

excerpt: Many lower-sodium salt substitutes use potassium chloride in place of some sodium chloride. They can reduce sodium intake, but they may taste more bitter or metallic and are not appropriate for everyone, especially people with impaired potassium excretion.
content_html:
A salt substitute may look almost identical to table salt while changing a nutrient that matters clinically. Many products replace part or all of the sodium chloride with potassium chloride, cutting sodium but increasing potassium.

Potassium chloride provides salty taste without sodium

Potassium chloride can mimic part of salt's taste and is used in lower-sodium products and household salt substitutes. FDA allows the alternate name “potassium salt” in certain food-label contexts to help consumers recognize its function.

The taste is not perfectly identical

Potassium chloride can introduce bitter or metallic notes, especially at higher replacement levels. Manufacturers often blend it with sodium chloride or other flavor strategies rather than replacing every gram of salt.

Lower sodium can be useful, but potassium changes the safety question

WHO recommends potassium-containing lower-sodium salt substitutes for adults in the general population as a sodium-reduction strategy. The recommendation does not apply to people with kidney impairment or other conditions that compromise potassium excretion, because excessive potassium can cause dangerous hyperkalemia.

Check both the ingredient list and your own medical context

If you take medicines or have a condition that affects potassium balance, ask a clinician before using potassium-based salt substitutes routinely. A salt substitute is not simply “healthier salt”; it is a different mineral formulation with different advantages and cautions.

faq.question: What is in a salt substitute?
faq.answer: Many products contain potassium chloride instead of some or all sodium chloride, though formulations vary.

faq.question: Do salt substitutes lower sodium?
faq.answer: Potassium-based substitutes can substantially lower sodium when they replace sodium chloride rather than being added on top of it.

faq.question: Who should be cautious with potassium salt substitutes?
faq.answer: People with kidney impairment or other conditions or medicines that impair potassium excretion should seek medical guidance because of hyperkalemia risk.
